Schmitt is referring to W. E. Hall, A Treatise on International Law, 8th ed., ed. A. Pearce Higgins, Oxford 1924. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 25814.
the feast of the Leviathan — See Leviathan, p. 18.
Köppelsbleek, the Schinderkuhle — Terms from Ernst Jünger’s story Auf den Marmorklippen (On the Marble Cliffs).
Touching, Gerhard Ritter — Schmitt is referring to Gerhard Ritter, Machtstaat und Utopie. Vom Streit um die Dämonie der Macht seit Machiavelli und Morus, 3rd and 4th ed., Munich/Berlin 1943.
Schmitt’s copy, inscribed by the author, survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 24136.

this Californian radio hero — Schmitt is targeting Thomas Mann and his broadcasts Deutsche Hörer! (“German Listeners!”), in which Mann regularly addressed the German people over the BBC from October 1940 to May 1945.
the creature of the Word in Konrad Weiß — See Konrad Weiß, “Kreatur des Wortes,” in Der Ring 4, 1931, pp. 901–903.
Th. Haecker’s attack on my Concept of the Political — Haecker criticized Schmitt for speaking of the enemy but not of the friend.
See Theodor Haecker, Was ist der Mensch, Leipzig 1933, pp. 71 ff.
the weakling Maritain and his hate-filled Raïssa — Jacques Maritain (1882–1973), French Thomist philosopher, had been a friend of Schmitt during the 1920s.
Their friendship ended because of Schmitt’s involvement with National Socialism. Schmitt placed much of the blame for the break on Maritain’s Jewish wife, Raïssa.
On the relationship between Schmitt and Maritain, see Piet Tommissen, “Neue Bausteine zu einer wissenschaftlichen Biographie Carl Schmitts,” in Schmittiana V, 1996, pp. 210–213.
“Now you stand naked, naked as at birth, in barren expanses” — From Theodor Däubler’s poem “Perseus.” The original has “Now” in the sense of Nun rather than Jetzt.
See Theodor Däubler, Der sternhelle Weg, Leipzig 1919, p. 71.
everything has already been accomplished, and you only answer — A passage frequently quoted by Schmitt after 1945, from Konrad Weiß’s poem “Klage über die Schöpfung.”
So the mind, the more it searches for itself, leads the soul from dark captivity into the world. Do what you must: it has always already been accomplished, and you only answer.
Magnificent, Gueydan … — The quotations come from a manuscript by Gueydan titled Pensées d’un dékan. The manuscript is not preserved in Schmitt’s papers.
See below, p. 122, entry for 11 June 1948.

reply concerning the state secretaries — Schmitt’s written answer to the question “Why did the state secretaries follow Hitler?”, which had been put to him by Robert Kempner, deputy chief prosecutor in the Nuremberg Wilhelmstrasse Trial.
It was first published under the title “Das Problem der Legalität” in Die neue Ordnung 5, 1950, pp. 270–275.

The planners rule — As early as 1933, in the essay “Machtpositionen des modernen Staates,” Schmitt had referred to Hans Freyer, Herrschaft und Planung. Zwei Grundbegriffe der politischen Ethik, Hamburg 1933.
The passage was later reprinted in Freyer, Herrschaft, Planung und Technik. Aufsätze zur politischen Soziologie, ed. Elfriede Üner, Weinheim 1987, p. 31:
“Where there is to be planning, there must be rule. It is not the planners who rule—that was the mistake of utopia. Rather, those who rule do the planning.”

Eduard Heimann — (1889–1967), social scientist. On the basis of his book Freedom and Order, New York 1947—German edition: Freiheit und Ordnung. Lehren aus dem Kriege, Berlin-Grunewald 1950—he gave lectures in several European countries during the spring and summer of 1948.
Däubler’s two brother-sonnets — In his collection Attische Sonette, Theodor Däubler dedicated the poem “An Phaidros” to Rudolf Pannwitz and “Pegasus” to Carl Schmitt.
Iranian Rhapsody — A cycle of poems in Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht, Geneva edition, Vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, pp. 265–341.
Kelsen’s reasoning … — In Kelsen’s view, the German state ceased to exist with the surrender of 8 May 1945 because state authority was thereafter exercised by the condominium of the Allied victors.
According to this view, every institutional connection between any future German state and the “Third Reich” was to be excluded once the Allied-dominated interim period had ended.

A broad counter-position developed against this doctrine of discontinuity. According to this opposing view, the German state had not ceased to exist but had merely become temporarily incapable of acting.
From 1947 onward this position was defended by Rolf Stödter, Wilhelm Grewe, Ulrich Scheuner, and others.

See Hans Kelsen, “The International Legal Status of Germany to be established immediately upon Termination of the War,” in American Journal of International Law 38, 1945, pp. 689 ff.; Kelsen, “The Legal Status of Germany According to the Declaration of Berlin,” ibid. 39, 1945, pp. 518 ff.; Rolf Stödter, Deutschlands Rechtslage, Hamburg 1948; Ulrich Scheuner, “Die staatsrechtliche Kontinuität in Deutschland,” in Die Öffentliche Verwaltung, 1950, No. 10, pp. 481 ff.
The paragraph corresponds to a section, though not an identical one, in Schmitt’s letter to Ernst Jünger of 11 June 1948.
the primal dissonance of nothing’s chirping — From Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht, Geneva edition, Vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, Der äthiopische Totentanz, pp. 160 f.:
“Dwarf, whirling runt,” I cried, “amuse yourself freely; cheat Death in the dance of whatever you rise to gain, and grow fat and lusty:

Let the primal dissonance of nothing’s chirping sound loudly in you; let it come from your own breast! Dance, dance, delouse the world, rid it of bedbugs; hey, black dwarf, tar-greasy and soot-thick, covered in the black shine of coal, your head shrivels up, your body grows crusted, and around you rolls a masked dance!”
Humbert Clérissac — (1864–1914), Dominican priest, author of Le mystère de l’église, published in 1914.
German edition: Das Geheimnis der Kirche, ed., trans., and annotated by Rudolf Michael Schmitz, Studi tomistici 23, Vatican City 1984.
Denis de Rougemont — (1906–1985), Swiss essayist. D. de Rougemont, La part du diable, New York 1942 and later editions. German edition: Der Anteil des Teufels, Munich 1999.
Gueydan, pensées d’un Dékan — Not identified.
that Nietzsche had fathered Hitler — See Ernst Niekisch, Deutsche Daseinsverfehlung, Aktuelle Kulturreihe, Berlin 1946.
Schmitt owned two copies, RW 265 Nos. 23051 and 23052.
Leon Trotsky wrote in 1923 … — Schmitt quotes inaccurately from Trotsky’s Literatur und Revolution, in Frida Rubiner’s German translation, Vienna 1924, RW 579 No. 1118.
The relevant passage, pp. 177–179, correctly reads:
“Human beings first drove blind elemental forces out of production and ideology, replacing barbaric routine with scientific technology and religion with science.

Then they drove the unconscious out of politics: first by overthrowing monarchy and the estates through democracy and rationalist parliamentarism, and finally through the transparently clear dictatorship of the soviets.

Blind elemental force weighs most heavily on economic relations—but human beings are driving it out there as well through the socialist organization of the economy. This makes a radical transformation of traditional family life possible.
Finally, in the deepest and darkest corner of the unconscious, elemental self, human nature itself lies asleep.
Is it not obvious that the greatest efforts of scientific thought and creative initiative will eventually be directed there?
Surely humanity did not stop crawling on its belly before God, kings, and capital only to surrender afterward to the blind laws of heredity and blind sexual selection!

Liberated humanity will want to achieve a greater balance in the functioning of its organs, a more even development and use of its tissues, and thereby confine fear of death within the limits of a useful biological response to danger.

For there can be no doubt that the extraordinary disharmony of the human being—both anatomical and physiological—the extraordinary unevenness in the development and wearing-out of organs and tissues, gives the instinct for life that cramped, pathological, hysterical form we call the fear of death: a fear that clouds reason and feeds stupid and degrading fantasies about an afterlife.

Human beings will set themselves the task of becoming masters of their own feelings, of raising their instincts to the highest level of consciousness and making them transparently clear, of extending the guiding threads of the will beneath the threshold of consciousness, and in this way of raising themselves to a higher level of awareness.
In other words, humanity will create a higher social-biological type—or, if one prefers, a superhuman.
The average human being will rise to the level of an Aristotle, a Goethe, a Marx.
Above that mountain ridge, new peaks will rise.”
“Hail to you, resplendent earth” — From Richard Wagner, Siegfried, Act III, Scene 3. A piano reduction survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 No. 26258.
In Dostoevsky, Kirillov says … — Schmitt quotes Dostoevsky from Walter Schubart, Dostojewski und Nietzsche. Symbolik ihres Lebens, Lucerne 1939, p. 47.
In Dostoevsky, according to E. K. Rahsin’s translation, the sentence reads:
“Man will be God and will change physically.”
Fyodor M. Dostoevsky, Die Dämonen, trans. E. K. Rahsin, Frankfurt am Main, c. 1992, p. 155.
Renan said — Ernest Renan (1823–1892), French scholar of religion and historian.
Renan made this often-repeated remark to the nationalist politician Paul Déroulède in 1883.
To Hans Beyer — Hans Joachim Beyer (1908–1971), historian and active National Socialist. He was an SS-Hauptsturmführer and a close associate of Reinhard Heydrich.
In 1940 he became a professor at Friedrich Wilhelm University in Berlin, in 1941 at Posen, and in 1943 at Prague.
After the war he became press spokesman for the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Schleswig-Holstein, and from 1951 he was a professor at the teacher-training college in Flensburg.

For more on him, see Stephan Linck, Neue Anfänge? Der Umgang der Evangelischen Kirche mit der NS-Vergangenheit und ihr Verhältnis zum Judentum. Die Landeskirchen in Nordelbien, Vol. 1, 1945–1965, Kiel 2013.
Beyer’s letter of 12 June 1948, to which Schmitt was replying, survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 No. 1318.
“Haecker’s thought … a more genuinely Catholic sharpening” — The correct passage reads:
“On closer examination, however, Haecker’s thought now belongs essentially to the Catholic literary movement as well.

It did not arise from that movement, because Haecker entered it as an outsider. Nor did it take part in the movement’s earlier opposition between a ‘classicist’ neutralization and a ‘Gothic’ realization.
But it is now struggling toward a more genuinely Catholic sharpening.

The movement itself is in many places turning, out of a barrenness in its creaturely and historical understanding, from the Word to language, from particularity to universality, and from a neutralized form of life to political confession. Much the same can also be said more generally about the intellectual and artistic decisions of the older generation.
Haecker’s thought now takes part in this struggle toward a more genuinely Catholic sharpening.”
Konrad Weiß, “Die Kreatur des Wortes,” in Der Ring (Berlin) 4, 1931, No. 48, p. 902.
Reprinted in Literaturwissenschaftliches Jahrbuch der Görres-Gesellschaft, New Series 12, 1971, pp. 311–315.
On Güllich — Hans Güllich, a first lieutenant on the Eastern Front during the Second World War.
Schmitt is referring to Güllich’s text titled “Lagebeurteilung,” which Güllich sent to Jünger and Jünger passed on to Schmitt.
Wilhelm Schmitz — (1912–?), jurist and industrialist who supported Schmitt after 1945.
See W. Schmitz, “Zur Geschichte der Academia Moralis,” in Schmittiana IV, 1994, pp. 119–156.
G. Radbruch’s favorable review of this book — Karl Schultes’s Der Niedergang des staatsrechtlichen Denkens im Faschismus, Weimar 1947; see the note above to p. 103.
Gustav Radbruch praised it in the Süddeutsche Juristenzeitung, Vol. 3, No. 5, 1948, pp. 223 f., as
“a work much needed for the cleansing of political thought. Heine’s phrase ‘No talent, but character’ could be applied here in reverse.”
“Idea and Reality of the Free German League” — Ernst Rudolf Huber, Idee und Realität eines Freideutschen Bundes, typescript in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 No. 20250.
